correctness.rationale: For every fixed \(n\ge2\), independent Rayleigh squares normalized by their sum are \(\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1)\). This yields an exact linear-at-origin one-coordinate density with coefficient \(c=(n-1)/n\) and pair intersection \(O(\varepsilon^4)\). The samplewise Laplace endpoint is \(2/n\) times the squared reciprocal-coordinate sum; a finite dependent one-large-coordinate argument gives tail coefficient \(c/z\) and the exact \(q<1\) moment boundary. Diagonal kernel second moments equal \(ct^2\log(1/t)+O(t^2)\) while cross moments are \(O(t^2)\), giving \(\mathbb ER_{n,a}=(2c\log a+O(1))/a^3\). A standalone checker reproduced 25 independent deterministic quadrature, root and samplewise comparisons for the two-sample case. Finite experiments do not substitute for the proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The general Stein fixed-point characterizations subsume the test construction, not this fixed-n Rayleigh moment trichotomy. General Laplace/Abelian identities would turn an established small-t expansion into the mean coefficient but do not independently supply the model-specific diagonal logarithm, exact Dirichlet dependence, or one-large-coordinate tail constant. Gaussian and Gamma tests are not the same statistic after changing variables: their empirical score and scale normalization differ.

originality.rationale: The original 2022 Rayleigh paper defines the statistic and treats \(n\to\infty\) at fixed bandwidth, not fixed \(n\) at large bandwidth. Broader Stein fixed-point and Gamma/normal-test papers give context but not the exact fitted-Rayleigh reciprocal-Dirichlet tail or logarithmic expectation. The samplewise Laplace limit is elementary from the definition; the new scientific contribution is the combined sharp infinite-mean tail and log-scale expectation. Searches against public literature and published research records found no directly covering result, with historical-priority risk stated.

value.rationale: For a published, used scale-invariant Rayleigh goodness-of-fit statistic, the finite-sample large-bandwidth regime has an unexpected disagreement between the almost-sure normalization and its mean. The exact heavy-tail constant, moment threshold and logarithmic expectation quantify calibration failure from extremely small fitted observations. This is a natural parameter endpoint of an existing test, rather than an arbitrary special sample size or routine numerical gain; no assertion about power or a full joint asymptotic theory is made.
